title: Newton's Laws of Motion
summary: Newton's three laws govern dynamics: an object keeps its velocity unless a net force acts (inertia); $\vec F_{net}=m\vec a$; and forces come in equal-and-opposite pairs. Free-body diagrams turn a situation into equations.

Newton's first law.plain: Inertia: no net force ⇒ constant velocity.

Newton's second law.plain: Net force equals mass times acceleration.

Newton's third law.plain: Every force has an equal, opposite reaction.

free-body diagram.plain: A sketch of all forces on one object.

net force.plain: The vector sum of all forces.

mass vs weight.plain: Amount of matter vs gravitational force on it.
mass vs weight.in_class: $W=mg$; mass is constant, weight varies with $g$.

normal force.plain: Support force perpendicular to a surface.
normal force.in_class: Adjusts to prevent objects sinking through surfaces.

concept_sections.heading: First law: inertia
concept_sections.explanation: Without a net force, an object's velocity stays constant — at rest or moving straight at constant speed. Motion doesn't need a force to continue, only to change.
math_steps: Check whether the net force is zero.
A force is needed only to change motion.

concept_sections.heading: Second law: $F=ma$
concept_sections.explanation: The net force equals mass times acceleration. Solve problems by summing forces along each axis and setting $\sum F=ma$.

concept_sections.heading: Free-body diagrams
concept_sections.explanation: Isolate one object and draw every force acting on it (gravity, normal, tension, friction, applied). This converts the physics into solvable equations.
math_steps: Choose axes and resolve into components.

concept_sections.heading: Third law: action–reaction
concept_sections.explanation: Forces occur in pairs: if A pushes B, B pushes A equally and oppositely. The pair acts on different objects, so they don't cancel on one object.
math_steps: The forces are equal and opposite.

concept_sections.heading: Weight and normal force
concept_sections.explanation: Weight is $W=mg$. The normal force is the surface's perpendicular support; on a flat surface with no vertical acceleration it equals the weight (or its perpendicular component on an incline).
math_steps: Balance vertical forces if no vertical acceleration.

real_world_examples.title: Seatbelts and inertia
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Your body continues forward by inertia (first law) until the belt applies a force.

real_world_examples.title: Rocket propulsion
real_world_examples.scenario: A rocket pushes gas out the back.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: By the third law, the gas pushes the rocket forward.

real_world_examples.title: An elevator ride
real_world_examples.scenario: You feel heavier as the elevator accelerates up.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The normal force exceeds your weight: $N-mg=ma$.
